content: In 2018, the WHO Global Leprosy Programme (GLP) plans to conduct a mid-term evaluation of its strategy to assess progress toward its targets and review evidence related to chemotherapy and diagnostics. For countries that have not yet achieved the elimination of leprosy as a public health problem at the first subnational level, implementing the actions recommended in the operational guidelines of the Global Strategy for 2016–2020 will support this goal. These actions include advocacy, health education, detection, and treatment. The use of the participation scale score will help assess the social participation of individuals affected by leprosy. Data availability will be critical to evaluate the level of stigma in communities, among patients, and healthcare workers. Partnerships with the private sector, including NGOs, community-based organizations (CBOs), and both traditional and allopathic private providers, will be essential for case detection, referral, care, and social support. Establishing coalitions against leprosy, either independently or as part of national coalitions addressing neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), tuberculosis, or disabilities, will also be vital. Access to testing for drug resistance and monitoring the number and proportion of drug-resistant cases will be prioritized. For countries or jurisdictions with populations under one million, the target for Grade 2 Disability (G2D) rates is not applicable. In countries where no pediatric G2D cases are detected, the target is zero pediatric cases. The Global Leprosy Strategy for 2016–2020 emphasizes early detection of all patients before disabilities develop, prompt treatment with a uniform multidrug therapy (MDT) regimen of shortened duration for multibacillary (MB) cases, and the inclusion of individuals affected by leprosy in program planning. It also focuses on enhancing research in prevention, new diagnostics, stigma reduction, and fostering broader partnerships. Efforts will be directed toward reducing the disease burden from various perspectives, such as disabilities among new patients (especially children) and the impact of stigma and discrimination in communities. A global research agenda will be developed to create new tools for interrupting transmission and reducing disability. Collaboration and information sharing among the scientific and public health communities involved in leprosy will be critical for implementing the global strategy. National governments bear the primary responsibility for leprosy control. Strengthening partnerships at national and subnational levels within countries will be necessary, involving various government departments and agencies. Governments will work with international organizations, including WHO, the private sector, NGOs, CBOs, and individuals affected by leprosy. These partnerships will support sustainability in expertise, resource mobilization, institutional development, stigma reduction, research, and community-based rehabilitation. Lessons from disability prevention strategies used in other NTDs and chronic noncommunicable disease programs should also be applied. To sustain expertise in leprosy, regional training centers and partner-run centers will be strengthened. New tools, such as e-learning and telemedicine, will be utilized where relevant. Nursing and medical school curricula will include leprosy to raise awareness among healthcare workers, even in low-endemic countries. Former patients and their families can serve as resources to maintain knowledge about the disease. Social workers and support departments will be engaged to promote societal inclusion for those affected. Quality leprosy services will focus on providing effective, efficient, and safe care that meets patients' needs and aligns with universal health coverage (UHC) goals. Special attention will be given to children and women, promoting early detection through periodic screening and facilitating diagnosis and access to care. Individuals affected by leprosy are valuable resources for leprosy programs and play a crucial role in control efforts. Strategies should build their capacity in advocacy and establish networks for psychosocial support to reduce emotional and economic distress, which often leads to depression and poverty. These individuals can also support early identification and improve treatment adherence. Organizations representing those affected by leprosy will be integral to these efforts. Promoting equity and social justice in all aspects of service provision for patients, their families, and communities will be encouraged. NGOs and civil society organizations can complement government actions to reduce stigma and advocate against discrimination. These aspects will receive equal focus in the leprosy agenda, referencing the United Nations Human Rights Council Resolution 29/5, which calls for the elimination of discrimination against individuals affected by leprosy and their families. Research to support leprosy control will focus on studying transmission, developing new diagnostic tools, prophylactic regimens, therapeutics, and innovative implementation strategies. The integration of leprosy into NTD programs will be assessed. Linkages among national and international research bodies, funding agencies, programs, universities, public laboratories, patient groups, and regulators will be established to secure funding and identify research initiatives. Results will be integrated into leprosy programs. The Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020 is built on three pillars: strengthening government ownership and partnerships, stopping leprosy and its complications, and stopping discrimination while promoting inclusion. Its goal is to reduce the global and local leprosy burden, aiming for zero children with leprosy-related disabilities, fewer than one new patient with leprosy-related deformities per million population, and the repeal of all laws allowing discrimination against leprosy patients. The strategy was endorsed by the WHO Technical Advisory Group on leprosy.
